research_text:
## Factual research brief — `java.security.KeyStore` / `KeyStoreSpec`

### 1. What `KeyStore` governs, and what this finding refers to

`java.security.KeyStore` is the Java API for a storage facility/repository of cryptographic keys and certificates. It manages entries such as `PrivateKeyEntry`, `SecretKeyEntry`, and `TrustedCertificateEntry`; implementations and persistence mechanisms are provider/type dependent. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))

The reported `InvalidSequenceOfMethodCalls` message is **not a documented Java exception or `KeyStore` API value**. In the supplied CrySL rule, it refers to whether the analyzer’s modeled method-call events satisfy the rule’s `ORDER` expression. The exact order condition in that rule is:

> `Get, Load, ((GetEntry?, GetKey) | (SetEntry, Store))*`

That is, for the rule’s modeled events, it expects `Get`, then `Load`, then zero or more repetitions of either:
* optional `GetEntry` followed by `GetKey`, or
* `SetEntry` followed by `Store`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl))

**No specific offending call or event can be identified from the detector message alone.** The message and supplied rule identify only the rejected abstract event trace; they do not provide the observed calls, resolved receiver, overload, object identity, analyzer version, or control/data-flow result. Under the supplied policy, that requires review rather than a conclusion about a particular use.

**Primary sources**
```text
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl
```

---

### 2. Documented correct and safe API usage; documented remediation

#### API lifecycle documented by Java

The Java API documentation says a `KeyStore` normally must be loaded before it can be accessed, unless it was already loaded when instantiated. A type-based factory such as `KeyStore.getInstance(String)` returns an object of the requested type; the normal subsequent operation is `load(...)`. The documentation shows loading from an input stream and says that passing `null` for the stream creates an empty keystore. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))

The API also documents two file-based `getInstance` overloads that return an **already loaded** keystore. These overloads probe the file, select a supporting provider, instantiate the keystore, and load its data; the Javadoc explicitly says they return a loaded object. They were introduced in Java 9. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))

Once loaded:

* `getKey(alias, char[] password)` returns the key associated with an alias; it can return `null` when the alias does not exist or is not key-related, and it throws `KeyStoreException` if the keystore has not been loaded. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))
* `getEntry(alias, ProtectionParameter)` retrieves an entry and permits a `null` protection parameter; it can return `null` if no entry exists, and throws `KeyStoreException` when the keystore is not loaded. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))
* `setEntry(alias, entry, ProtectionParameter)` saves an entry under an alias; it throws `KeyStoreException` if the keystore has not been loaded. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))
* `store(OutputStream, char[])` writes the keystore and protects its integrity using the supplied password; the password can be `null` only where the implementation does not support or require an integrity check. `store(LoadStoreParameter)` can throw `UnsupportedOperationException` if storing is unsupported. Both documented overloads require an initialized/loaded keystore. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))

The Javadoc sample’s lifecycle is: instantiate; load; retrieve an entry; modify/set an entry; store; and destroy the `PasswordProtection` object in a `finally` block. It further notes that load, entry-protection, and store protection may use different passwords or protection parameters. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))

#### “Recommended remediation” in official sources

The Java API does **not** document a diagnostic named `InvalidSequenceOfMethodCalls` and does **not** prescribe a universal remediation for a CrySL finding. Therefore, no official-source basis exists to say that a particular code change is the recommended remediation for this finding.

The documented operational corrections are limited to the API’s stated prerequisites and alternatives:

1. **For a newly instantiated, type-based `KeyStore`:** load it before accessing, changing, or storing it; use `load(null, ...)` to create an empty in-memory keystore. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))  
2. **For the Java 9+ file-based `getInstance(File, ...)` overloads:** do not add a load merely because of the generic lifecycle description—the API documents that these overloads already return a loaded keystore. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))  
3. **For persistence:** use a supported `store` overload only where the selected provider/type supports it; the API expressly permits `UnsupportedOperationException` from `store(LoadStoreParameter)`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))

This is API semantics, not a determination that any particular reported sequence is incorrect.

---

### 3. Compatibility when usage changes

#### Persisted formats

A keystore type defines its storage/data format and the algorithms used for protecting keys and keystore integrity. Oracle’s JCA reference states that keystore implementations of different types are **not compatible**. Accordingly, changing type/provider can change the persisted format and protection semantics. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))

The `KeyStore` class itself does not define a universal on-disk representation. The API says persistence and persistence mechanisms are unspecified, allowing implementations including files, smart cards, and other cryptographic engines. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))

#### Wire / transport formats

`KeyStore` itself does not define a network wire protocol. The closest documented portable format is `PKCS12`: Oracle documents it as a cross-platform format based on the RSA PKCS#12 Personal Information Exchange Syntax Standard and intended for storage or transport of private keys, certificates, and miscellaneous secrets. That describes the **keystore format**, not a `KeyStore` network protocol. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))

#### Platform and version support

* `KeyStore` has existed since Java 1.2. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))
* Java platform implementations are required to support the standard `PKCS12` keystore type; other type availability is implementation/release dependent. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))
* Oracle documents `PKCS12` as the default and recommended keystore type from JDK 9 onward; the earlier default was proprietary `JKS`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))
* `KeyStore.getInstance(File, char[])` and `KeyStore.getInstance(File, LoadStoreParameter)` are documented as available since Java 9. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))
* `load(LoadStoreParameter)`, `store(LoadStoreParameter)`, `getEntry`, and `setEntry` are documented since Java 1.5. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))

#### Documented migration paths

Oracle documents `keytool -importkeystore` as the general tool-supported path to import an entire keystore, including keys and certificates, into another keystore, including one of a different type. It states that destination entries retain aliases and protection passwords for secret/private keys, subject to password recovery and alias-conflict handling. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/man/keytool.html))

Oracle also documents a specific JKS-to-JCEKS conversion capability: the JCEKS implementation can parse and convert JKS files, and the guide describes upgrading by changing a private-key entry password with JCEKS selected as the store type. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))

The official material does **not** guarantee that every provider-specific keystore, entry type, protection parameter, or hardware-backed/non-extractable key can be migrated to every destination type. Provider support and recoverability remain limiting conditions; `keytool` itself documents prompting if it cannot recover source private or secret keys. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/man/keytool.html))

**Primary sources**
```text
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/man/keytool.html
```

---

### 4. Exact matching rule in the supplied `KeyStore.crysl`

**Source examined**
```text
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl
```

#### Governing receiver type

The rule begins:

> `SPEC java.security.KeyStore`

Thus, the source declares the governed API type as `java.security.KeyStore`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl))

#### Verbatim matching/event clause

The exact `EVENTS` clause is:

```text
EVENTS
	g1: getInstance(type);
	g2: getInstance(type, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;
	l1: load(fileInput, passwordIn);
	l2: load(paramLoad);
	Load := l1 | l2;

	s1: store(paramStore);
	s2: store(fileOutput, passwordOut);
	Store := s1 | s2;

	ge1: getEntry(aliasGet, protParamGet);
	GetEntry := ge1;

	se1: setEntry(aliasSet, entry, protParamSet);
	SetEntry := se1;

	gk1: key = getKey(alias, passwordKey);
	GetKey := gk1;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl))

Therefore, the source lists these method names/events:

| Rule event | Method pattern(s) stated in source |
|---|---|
| `Get` | `getInstance(type)`; `getInstance(type, _)` |
| `Load` | `load(fileInput, passwordIn)`; `load(paramLoad)` |
| `Store` | `store(paramStore)`; `store(fileOutput, passwordOut)` |
| `GetEntry` | `getEntry(aliasGet, protParamGet)` |
| `SetEntry` | `setEntry(aliasSet, entry, protParamSet)` |
| `GetKey` | `key = getKey(alias, passwordKey)` |

The declared object variables constrain the parameter forms used by those event patterns. For example, `type`, aliases, and `key` are declared as `java.lang.String`/`java.security.Key` as applicable; passwords are `char[]`; the input and output are `java.io.InputStream` and `java.io.OutputStream`; entries and parameters use nested `KeyStore` types. The second `getInstance` argument is written `_`, so the source does not name or type-constrain that argument in the event pattern itself. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl))

#### Evaluated condition

The rule then evaluates the following order and constraints:

```text
ORDER
	Get, Load, ((GetEntry?, GetKey) | (SetEntry, Store))*
CONSTRAINTS
	type in {"JCEKS", "JKS", "DKS", "PKCS11", "PKCS12"};
	neverTypeOf[passwordIn, java.lang.String];
	neverTypeOf[passwordOut, java.lang.String];
	neverTypeOf[passwordKey, java.lang.String];
	notHardCoded[passwordIn];
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl))

In source terms, that is an order condition plus constraints on the `type` variable and the three password variables. The source also declares postconditions under `ENSURES`, but those are not part of the `ORDER` condition. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl))

#### Can it match a merely same-named method on another API?

**No, not according to the scope stated by this source.** The rule is explicitly declared as:

> `SPEC java.security.KeyStore`

The event method names occur under that specification, rather than as unqualified global rules. Therefore the source text governs `java.security.KeyStore`, not a method that merely shares a name on an unrelated receiver type. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl))

**Important source limit:** the raw `.crysl` file does not itself specify the analyzer’s exact type-resolution, inheritance, dispatch, Kotlin, reflection, interprocedural, or unresolved-call behavior. It establishes the declared `SPEC` type and event syntax, but not the implementation semantics of a particular detector release. Hence, whether a given analyzer actually resolved a call as a `java.security.KeyStore` receiver cannot be determined from this source or detector message alone.
